summary: The one-week visibility window this test pins down is not stated by any claim of WB-800.
evidence: The two tests of this unit are covered by WB-800#c3 ("Added `rejectedApplicationsWithOtherReason` method to get rejected applications data with test-cases"); both carry an @see back to that controller method. One of them, however, asserts a product rule none of the six claims states: applications rejected under OtherReasonsRejectionSpecification more than a week ago must not be returned (assertJsonCount(0, 'data') for decisions created two weeks ago). WB-800#c1 speaks only of a new route "to fetch rejected applications" and WB-800#c3 only of a method "to get rejected applications data"; neither mentions any recency cutoff, and no note stands against the issue key. The implementation side matches the test (app/Http/Controllers/Retailer/ApplicationActionController.php:138 computes now()->startOfDay()->subWeek() and line 148 filters lastDecision.created_at by it), so this is an agreed behaviour of the change, not a test-only invention. What cannot be established from the diff and the issue text is where the window comes from and whether one week is the intended figure: the test name says "7 days" while the code measures from the start of today, which makes the effective window 7 to 8 days depending on the time of day. Asking the author to confirm the intended cutoff, and to record it on the issue, is what settles this.

summary: The seven-day recency window applied to the rejection decision is not stated by any claim of WB-800; only the test name records it.
evidence: The unit maps to claim WB-800#c3 ("Added `rejectedApplicationsWithOtherReason` method to get rejected applications data with test-cases"), and the filter on the decision type matches claim WB-800#c1's wording "rejected-by-other-reason". No claim of the round, and no line of the issue text (the changelog entry the claims are drawn from, changelogs/unreleased/WB-800-rejected-application-with-reason-others.md:6-14), mentions any time limit. The method nevertheless narrows the result set to applications whose last decision was created on or after now()->startOfDay()->subWeek() (line 138 and line 148), which is a business rule the endpoint's callers depend on: an application rejected for other reasons eight days ago is invisible. The only written record of that rule inside the pull request is the name of the test at tests/Feature/Retailer/ApplicationActionControllerTest.php:2339 and the @see docblock at line 131; no note is recorded against the issue key. This reads as intent that never reached the tracker rather than a defect, so it goes to the author: which claim is the seven-day window meant to satisfy, and is a week the intended boundary (the window is also anchored at start of day, so the effective cut-off runs from 7 to 8 days back depending on the request time)?

summary: The new lastDecision() relation shares its name with the existing getLastDecisionAttribute accessor (Application.php:265) but means something different. Should the retailer listing reuse the accessor's definition of 'last decision', or should the relation get a distinct name and a subject filter?
evidence: Application already has getLastDecisionAttribute (app/Models/Application.php:265), which exposes 'last_decision'. It returns the last Farmer-subject decision from decisionsWithTrashed, so soft-deleted decisions count. The new relation hasOne(Decision::class)->latest() has no subject filter and skips soft-deleted rows. Because Eloquent's getAttribute checks for a get mutator under the studly name first, both $application->lastDecision and $application->last_decision go to the accessor. The relation can only be reached through lastDecision() or whereHas/with('lastDecision'). This PR checks the same 'rejected for other reasons' rule both ways. SendRejectionNotificationToFarmerAction.php:29 and SendRejectionNotificationToRetailerAction.php:29 read $application->last_decision (the accessor). Retailer ApplicationActionController.php:145 filters on whereHas('lastDecision') (the relation). When the newest decision is a guarantor decision, or the farmer decision was soft-deleted, the notification and the retailer listing can disagree. The pattern $application->decisions()->forFarmer(...)->latest()->first() also appears in several actions (e.g. app/Machines/Application/Actions/SendMissingInfoNotificationToSMAction.php:21). The author may have a reason to include guarantor decisions that the diff does not show.

summary: `lastDecision` is `hasOne(Decision::class)->latest()`, which only orders the query and does not limit it to the latest row, so the only caller's `whereHas('lastDecision', ...)` matches any decision of the application, not its last one.
evidence: The claim adds a relation meaning 'the last decision'. `latest()` adds `ORDER BY created_at DESC` and nothing else. That is enough for lazy loading (`->first()`), but the only caller of the relation is `whereHas('lastDecision', ...)` at app/Http/Controllers/Retailer/ApplicationActionController.php:145. Eloquent compiles that to `EXISTS (select * from application_decisions where application_id = applications.id and type = 'OtherReasonsRejectionSpecification' and created_at >= ?)`. The existence subquery has no LIMIT and no max-per-parent constraint, so the ORDER BY does nothing. Here is an input that reaches it: a rejected application with an OtherReasonsRejectionSpecification decision from three days ago, followed by a newer decision of another type (for example a later re-scoring rejected by MissingInfoSpecification). The endpoint `retailer.rejected-by-other-reason-applications` still lists it, and the WB-800 notification rule says it should not, because the last decision is not 'other reason'. The same applies to any application with repeated decisions. The codebase already has the idiom that does constrain existence queries to the latest row: `hasOne(...)->latestOfMany()` at app/Models/Order.php:492 and app/Models/Product.php:350. Laravel 11 (composer.json:30) supports it. The other 'last decision' lookups (for example app/Machines/Application/Actions/RejectedToApprovedTransitionAction.php:40 and app/Machines/Application/Actions/SendRejectedNotificationByReasonAction.php:23) use `decisions()->latest()->first()`. That form is a real single-row fetch, so it does not have this problem. I checked them and they are not affected. The new PR tests only create applications with one decision each, so they cannot tell 'last' from 'any'.

summary: No test exercises the 'latest' part of the new lastDecision relation: every test that reaches it creates exactly one decision per application, so dropping or inverting ->latest() would leave the suite green.
evidence: lastDecision is only consumed at app/Http/Controllers/Retailer/ApplicationActionController.php:145 through whereHas('lastDecision', ...). The two tests covering that endpoint (tests/Feature/Retailer/ApplicationActionControllerTest.php:2290 and :2339) build applications via ApplicationFactory::withRejectionDecisionType (database/factories/ApplicationFactory.php:381), which creates a single decision; rejected() (ApplicationFactory.php:340) creates none. With one decision per application, 'last decision' and 'any decision' are indistinguishable, so the ordering is never observed. Worse, Eloquent's whereHas compiles an EXISTS subquery that ignores the relation's ORDER BY and does not limit to one row, so an application whose older decision is OtherReasonsRejection (within 7 days) but whose newest decision is a different type is still returned. A test with two decisions of different types would expose this. Not established by experiment; see proposals x6501 (gap) and x6502 (mutation).

summary: The assertNotSentTo block cannot fail after assertNothingSent, so its callback never runs and asserts nothing.
evidence: Line 79 calls Notification::assertNothingSent(), which passes only when the fake recorded no notification at all. Lines 80-87 then call Notification::assertNotSentTo() with a callback checking $notification->applicationId and $notification->afterCommit. NotificationFake::assertNotSentTo asserts that the count of matching sent notifications is 0; once assertNothingSent has passed there is nothing for it to match, so the callback is never invoked and the block cannot fail for any reason line 79 has not already caught. The consequence is that the test appears to assert something about the notification's payload and does not: if SendRejectionNotificationToRetailerAction were changed to send an ApplicationRejectedNotification with a different applicationId or without afterCommit(), the failure would come from line 79, and the callback would still never execute. The guard itself is genuinely covered (the setup is not vacuous: withRejectionDecisionType stores class_basename(OtherReasonsRejectionSpecification::class) with subject Farmer, which is what Application::getLastDecisionAttribute() returns, so dropping the condition in the action makes line 79 fail) - the defect is confined to the dead block. summary: The new public parameter `string $decision` holds a RejectionSpecification class name, not a decision, which is the exact case the project's variable-named-for-its-value rule describes.
evidence: withRejectionDecisionType(string $decision, ...) is called with a specification class (tests pass OtherReasonsRejectionSpecification::class) and the body uses it as `$decision::calculateBlockingPeriod($application)` and `class_basename($decision)`, while the same closure builds an ApplicationDecision row whose 'decision' key is 0 (line 387). A specification held in a variable called $decision reads as a decision at every later line.' summary: The negative fixtures in both new tests are never REJECTED, so neither test exercises the 'other reason' decision-type filter, the retailer filter or the last-decision semantics of rejectedApplicationsWithOtherReason.
evidence: The distractor applications are built with forStatus(randomElement(ApplicationStatus::cases() minus waitingApplicationStatusesList())), and waitingApplicationStatusesList() includes ApplicationStatus::REJECTED (test line 2414). The controller already drops every one of these distractors through ->rejected() (app/Http/Controllers/Retailer/ApplicationActionController.php:142), before the whereHas on lastDecision with type = OtherReasonsRejectionSpecification (line 147) ever runs. The only REJECTED applications in either test carry an OtherReasonsRejectionSpecification decision, so if you delete the type predicate on line 147, or the retailer_id predicate on line 143, both tests still pass: 2-5 rows in the first test and 0 in the second. The same fixture pattern is at lines 2363-2380 in the second test. Also, lastDecision is hasOne(Decision::class)->latest() (app/Models/Application.php:1062), and whereHas does not keep the latest() ordering as a 'last row only' constraint. So an application with an earlier OtherReasons decision and a newer decision of another type still matches, and no fixture here covers that case. The second test also checks only a 2-week-old decision, not the 7-day boundary its name claims. Was it deliberate that no REJECTED application has a different decision type, belongs to another retailer or has a newer non-OtherReasons decision? Without one, the claim's 'with test-cases' does not pin the filtering it describes.
suggestion: Add a REJECTED application for the same retailer with a decision of another RejectionSpecification type, one for another retailer with an OtherReasons decision, and one whose OtherReasons decision is followed by a newer decision of another type. Assert that the response contains only the intended IDs, not just a count.

summary: whereHas('lastDecision') does not test the latest decision: Application::lastDecision() is a plain hasOne()->latest(), so the existence subquery matches ANY non-deleted decision of type OtherReasonsRejectionSpecification created in the last week, and a rejected application whose latest decision is a different rejection is still listed.
evidence: Application::lastDecision() (app/Models/Application.php:1060-1063) is `hasOne(Decision::class)->latest()`, not latestOfMany(); in whereHas Eloquent turns it into `EXISTS (select * from application_decisions where application_id = applications.id and type = ? and created_at >= ? order by created_at desc)`, where the ORDER BY does not narrow the rows, so the filter means "has some OtherReasons decision this week". Applications do accumulate several decisions: RejectedToApprovedTransition (e.g. app/Services/ApplicationStrategy/ForwardSale/StateMachine/Transitions/RejectedToApprovedTransition.php:79) adds an approval decision to a rejected application, and later rejections add further decisions, some with a non-Farmer subject (RejectAction takes subject from the guard data). Path: admin rejects with OtherReasons (decision A), application is moved to approved (decision B), then rejected again for another reason, e.g. fraud via RejectByFraudAction (decision C), all within 7 days -> status REJECTED, latest decision C is not OtherReasons, yet the endpoint returns the application as 'rejected by other reason'. The same rule appears in two other places in this PR, SendRejectionNotificationToFarmerAction.php:29 and SendRejectionNotificationToRetailerAction.php:29 (both checked). They use the last_decision accessor (Application.php:265-274), which takes the LAST decision including trashed ones, filtered to subject Farmer. So for this application the notification actions treat it as a normal rejection and send the notice, while this endpoint lists it as an other-reason rejection. The claim's 'rejected applications' with other reason rests on 'last decision', and the query does not enforce that. The added tests create exactly one decision per application, so they cannot tell the two meanings apart.
suggestion: Constrain on the actual latest Farmer-subject decision, matching the last_decision accessor, e.g. define a latestOfMany relation (`hasOne(Decision::class)->ofMany(['id' => 'max'], fn ($q) => $q->forSubject(ApplicationDecisionSubject::Farmer))`) and use it in whereHas, and add a test where an older OtherReasons decision is followed by a newer decision of another type.

summary: No test would notice the decision-type filter being dropped: no fixture has a rejected application whose decision is a type other than OtherReasonsRejectionSpecification.
evidence: Both new tests (ApplicationActionControllerTest.php:2290 and :2339) create the positive set with withRejectionDecisionType(OtherReasonsRejectionSpecification::class). The noise applications use forStatus(...) only, and ApplicationFactory::forStatus (database/factories/ApplicationFactory.php:77) creates no decision rows, so whereHas('lastDecision') already excludes them. Removing ->where('type', ...) would leave both assertJsonCount assertions unchanged. Not probed; mutation proposal x5801 would settle it.

summary: No test checks that a retailer cannot see another retailer's other-reason rejected applications, so the retailer_id scoping could be removed with the suite still green.
evidence: Every application in both new tests is created withRetailer($retailerUser->retailer); no fixture belongs to a different retailer. Dropping ->where('retailer_id', ...) would still return exactly the same rows, so both assertJsonCount assertions would still pass. This filter is the only tenant boundary on the endpoint. Not probed; mutation proposal x5802 would settle it.

summary: The notDemo() and rejected() scopes are unguarded: no fixture is a demo application or a non-rejected application that carries an OtherReasons decision.
evidence: All positive fixtures are rejected() and non-demo; the noise fixtures have no decision rows, so the whereHas already filters them out. Deleting ->rejected() or ->notDemo() changes no result in either new test. Not probed; mutation proposal x5803 would settle the rejected() half.

summary: No test covers an application with several decisions where an older one is OtherReasons and the latest is a different type, so the 'last decision' behaviour is unverified.
evidence: Application::lastDecision is hasOne(Decision::class)->latest() (app/Models/Application.php:1060). whereHas on it builds an EXISTS subquery that ignores the ordering, so it matches any decision, not just the latest one. Every fixture in the new tests has exactly one decision, so the tests cannot tell 'latest decision is OtherReasons' apart from 'any decision is OtherReasons'. The 7-day boundary is also only tested far from the edge (2 weeks old), not at startOfDay()->subWeek(). Not probed; gap proposal x5804 would settle the multi-decision case.
